title: Nazrin: An Atomic Neural Proof Automation Tactic in Lean 4
abstract: In Machine-Assisted Theorem Proving, a theorem proving agent searches for a sequence of expressions and tactics that can prove a statement in a proof assistant. In this work, we introduce several novel concepts and capabilities to address obstacles faced by machine-assisted theorem proving. We first present a set of atomic tactics, a small finite set of tactics capable of proving any provable statement in Lean. We then introduce a transposing atomization algorithm which turns arbitrary proof expressions into a series of atomic tactics. We next introduce the ExprGraph data structure, which provides a succinct representation for Lean expressions. Finally, we present the Nazrin Prover, short for Neural Atomizer for Inhabitation Problems, a graph neural network-based theorem proving agent using atomic tactics and ExprGraph. Nazrin circumvents many challenges faced by existing proving agents by exclusively dispatching atomic tactics, and it is robust enough to both train and evaluate on consumer-grade hardware. We demonstrate the potential of tools like Nazrin using theorems from Lean’s standard library and from Mathlib.

title: Stability and Reliability of Explainable AI in Cardiovascular Risk Prediction Models
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are a reason for deaths all around the world. This shows how important it is to find out who is atrisk. Machine learning models are really good at predicting risk, but they are so complex that it is hard to understand howthey work. This makes doctors not trust them much. There are techniques like Explainable AI that try to explain how thesemodels think, such as SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients. However, when you use these techniques, the results can bedifferent for cases or when you make small changes, which makes you wonder if they are stable and reliable. In our study,we looked at different models that predict risk, including logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and neuralnetworks. We used these models with known datasets like the Framingham Heart Study, MIMIC, and UK Biobank to seewhat was going on. For each model, we used Explainable AI methods to see which parts of the data were important andchecked how stable these explanations were when we changed the input a little bit or used different samples. We alsochecked if the explanations made sense for patients who were similar and asked doctors if they agreed with what themodels were saying. What we found was that simpler models gave us consistent explanations, but they were not asaccurate as the more complex models. On the one hand, complex models like ensemble trees and deep nets were moreaccurate, but their explanations varied more. We also saw that SHAP was better at giving us explanations that did notchange much more than methods like LIME. This tells us that just being able to explain something is not enough; we needto be able to trust these explanations. When we choose healthcare models, we should think about how stable theirexplanations are. It is very important to have explanations that make sense and are consistent so that doctors can trustthem and use them safely.

title: Cave Nectar Bat: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Cave Nectar Bat Behavior
abstract: This paper introduces "Cave Nectar Bat" (CNB), a new metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of cave nectar bats. These bats exhibit a unique strategy of navigating complex cave environments to locate nectar sources, relying heavily on acoustic cues and local exploration. CNB leverages this behavior to create a novel optimization algorithm designed for solving complex, non-linear optimization problems. The algorithm incorporates a "sound mapping" mechanism, mimicking the bats' use of echoes, to guide search and exploration. Furthermore, it utilizes a "pheromone deposition" system, analogous to the bats' communication, to reinforce promising solutions. The core of CNB is a dynamically adjusted exploration-exploitation balance, driven by simulated echo intensity and pheromone concentration. We present a theoretical analysis of CNB's convergence properties and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations on a range of benchmark optimization problems. Results show that CNB exhibits competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic algorithms, particularly in challenging, high-dimensional landscapes. The algorithm's adaptability and reliance on local information make it suitable for problems where global information is limited or unavailable.

title: Measuring What Was Said, Not Only How It Sounded: A Hybrid Deterministic and Generative Architecture for Automated Assessment of Children's Impromptu Speech
abstract: Automated speech coaching tools have converged on a narrow set of metrics: speaking rate, disfluency counts, and pause frequency. These are measured because they are cheap to measure, not because they are what makes a spoken argument good. The result is a category of products that can tell a speaker they said "um" eleven times but cannot tell them their argument was unsupported. This paper describes the architecture of a system that assesses both halves, for speakers aged 6 to 14. It advances four design claims: that delivery measurement should be deterministic rather than generative, since a language model receives text and cannot hear audio; that content quality is assessable and is the higher-value signal; that acoustic baselines must be within-subject when the speaker population is developmentally heterogeneous; and that withholding numeric scores from the end user is an assessment design decision rather than a presentation preference.

title: ## Caucasian Mountain Ground Squirrel Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper proposes a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the Caucasian Mountain Ground Squirrel (CMGS) algorithm, inspired by the foraging behavior of the Caucasian Mountain Ground Squirrel (Eliomys thapetes) in its native habitat. Squirrels exhibit a unique strategy for locating food sources amidst complex, uneven terrain. This algorithm leverages this strategy through a combination of exploration and exploitation phases, mimicking the squirrel's adaptive movement patterns. The core of the CMGS algorithm involves a virtual terrain representation, a movement strategy based on gradient estimation and obstacle avoidance, and an adaptive population management system. The algorithm is designed to be applicable to a broad range of optimization problems, including continuous and discrete. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through simulated tests on benchmark functions, comparing its performance against established metaheuristic techniques such as the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and the Genetic Algorithm (GA). The results indicate that the CMGS algorithm exhibits competitive performance and potential for further development.

title: ## Cape Genet Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm (CGMOA)
abstract: This paper presents the Cape Genet Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm (CGMOA), a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of Cape Genets. The algorithm incorporates key aspects of Cape Genet's hunting strategy, including social learning, territory defense, and opportunistic foraging, into a multi-objective optimization framework. CGMOA utilizes a population-based approach with a novel representation scheme mimicking the genetic structure of Cape Genet social groups. The algorithm's core components involve a dynamic territory assignment mechanism, a social learning component based on imitation of successful individuals, and an adaptive exploration-exploitation strategy influenced by the perceived resource availability. The performance of CGMOA is evaluated on a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions with reasonable computational cost. The algorithm's design aims to balance exploration and exploitation, leading to robust convergence and adaptability to diverse problem landscapes. Experimental results show CGMOA's competitive performance against established metaheuristic algorithms like NSGA-II and PSO, highlighting its potential for practical applications in various optimization domains.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding and Decoding: An Adaptive Topological Protocol
abstract: Quantum entanglement offers a revolutionary approach to information encoding and decoding, surpassing the limitations of classical methods. This paper introduces a novel quantum information encoding and decoding protocol leveraging the inherent properties of quantum topology. The core concept is the "拓扑自适应编码" (拓扑自适应编码) mechanism, which dynamically adjusts the topology of a quantum state through entanglement changes, rendering the protocol robust against environmental fluctuations. We present a theoretical framework for this protocol, detailing the mechanism, its potential advantages, and preliminary results demonstrating its adaptability. The proposed protocol represents a significant advance in quantum information security and communication, offering a fundamentally different approach to encoding and decoding with enhanced resilience.

title: Dynamic Memory Allocation and Quantum Computing Synergy
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum computing by integrating dynamic memory allocation techniques with quantum algorithms. The core idea is to leverage quantum entanglement to construct a dynamic memory structure for quantum data, enabling efficient storage and manipulation. We propose a framework where quantum algorithms operate directly on this dynamically structured memory, significantly improving both the efficiency and scalability of quantum computations. The theoretical foundations of this synergy are presented, outlining the mathematical framework and key concepts. The primary focus is on the optimization of quantum data storage and retrieval, addressing limitations inherent in traditional quantum memory models. The presented methodology offers a promising pathway for advancing quantum computing, particularly in scenarios demanding adaptable and resource-conscious quantum algorithms. The work details a method for representing quantum states within a dynamically allocated memory space, utilizing entanglement to facilitate rapid state access and modification. Mathematical notation is used throughout to formally define the concepts and algorithms.

title: Dynamic Topology of Quantum States: A Novel Mechanism for Quantum State Free Transitions
abstract: Quantum states exhibit remarkable fragility, making them highly susceptible to environmental perturbations. Conventional quantum state transition mechanisms often rely on static, deterministic processes, limiting the system's adaptability. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum state transition, leveraging dynamic topology to achieve free quantum state transitions. We propose a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the topology of the quantum state, allowing it to respond to environmental changes and facilitate intricate free jumps. This approach significantly enhances the system's robustness and potential for complex quantum operations. We detail the theoretical framework underpinning this dynamic topology, present the implementation of the mechanism, and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulation and analysis. The core of this research lies in the identification and utilization of topological properties to guide and control quantum state transitions, offering a fundamentally new pathway to quantum state freedom. We explore the implications of this approach for various quantum computing applications, including quantum error correction and the exploration of novel quantum algorithms.

title: ## Bolivian Grass Mouse Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the "Bolivian Grass Mouse Algorithm" (BGMA), inspired by the foraging behavior of the Bolivian Grass Mouse (Mus schimidtii). This algorithm leverages the mouse's efficient exploration and exploitation strategies in a complex and dynamic environment to solve complex optimization problems. BGMA incorporates elements of adaptive step size control, a novel mutation operator mimicking the mouse's movement pattern, and a dynamically adjusting population diversity mechanism. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on a range of benchmark functions, demonstrating its effectiveness and competitive capability compared to established metaheuristic methods such as the Genetic Algorithm and Particle Swarm Optimization. The core of the algorithm lies in its ability to balance exploration and exploitation effectively, leading to robust solutions across diverse problem landscapes. The algorithm's design prioritizes adaptability and resilience, mirroring the Bolivian Grass Mouse's survival strategies in its natural habitat. This research contributes a new approach to metaheuristic optimization, offering potential applications in various fields including engineering design, financial modeling, and machine learning.

title: Title: Modular Proof Systems for Complex Logic
abstract: The development of robust and scalable logic systems is a critical challenge in formal systems. Traditional proof systems often struggle with complex structures and rigorous verification. This paper proposes a novel modular proof system designed to address these challenges by enabling the construction of complex logical systems from smaller, independently verifiable modules. We outline a system that automatically generates and verifies logical statements based on a predefined set of modules, fostering a chain of logical proofs. The core mechanism centers on a modular architecture that promotes adaptability and simplifies the verification process. This system seeks to provide a foundation for complex logical reasoning and verification, offering a significant step towards more reliable and scalable formal systems.

title: CHATBOT DIAGNOSA GANGGUAN INTERNET MENGGUNAKAN NLP DAN FORWARD CHAINING PADA PT SOLO JALA BUANA
abstract: Perkembangan penggunaan internet semakin pesat meningkatkan kebutuhan pelanggan terhadap layanan internet yang cepat dan stabil. PT Solo Jala Buana sebagai penyedia layanan internet masih menghadapi kendala dalam penanganan keluhan pelanggan, seperti lamanya waktu respons customer service dan tingginya jumlah laporan gangguan yang diterima setiap hari. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengembangkan chatbot diagnosa gangguan internet dengan mengintegrasikan Natural Language Processing (NLP) dan metode Forward Chaining untuk membantu pelanggan memperoleh diagnosa awal beserta solusi penanganan secara otomatis. Pengembangan sistem menggunakan metode Waterfall meliputi analisis kebutuhan, perancangan sistem, implementasi, pengujian, dan pemeliharaan. Teknologi NLP digunakan untuk memproses masukan pengguna melalui tahapan case folding, tokenizing, filtering, dan stemming sehingga sistem mampu mengidentifikasi gejala gangguan internet dari kalimat yang diberikan pengguna. Metode Forward Chaining digunakan untuk melakukan proses inferensi berdasarkan basis pengetahuan dan rule base dalam menentukan jenis gangguan beserta solusi yang sesuai. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa chatbot mampu memahami keluhan pengguna, mengidentifikasi gejala, melakukan proses inferensi, menghasilkan diagnosa sesuai dengan aturan yang telah dirancang. Pengujian menggunakan metode Black Box Testing menunjukkan seluruh fungsi sistem berjalan sesuai kebutuhan fungsional. Dengan demikian, chatbot yang dikembangkan mampu membantu pelanggan memperoleh informasi, diagnosa awal, dan solusi secara cepat serta mendukung peningkatan efektivitas pelayanan pelanggan di PT Solo Jala Buana.

title: Adding an Epistemic Layer to DOLCE
abstract: Traditional approaches in applied ontology do not consider the dependency of property exemplification on their sources. However, there are cases where it is important to consider the subjective dimension of exemplification. For example, in engineering it is common to consider how sensors deliver outputs, or use algorithms that ascribe values to properties of the entities under analysis based on input data and calculations. Aiming to address such scenarios, we explore an approach to represent an epistemic view on property exemplification. Building on previous work, we discuss different ways in which this can be formally done in DOLCE, namely, by exploiting the representation of (standard) predication mechanisms, individual qualities, or concepts. The approach fits particularly well in applications where it is relevant to represent and reason over incoherent and even incompatible data, possibly originating from multiple sources, while preserving the consistency of the knowledge-base.

abstract: The existing methods for tabular data prediction primarily focus on classical classification and regression tasks. However, a type of data in the tabular data domain contains labels with an ordinal relationship, and its prediction task is called tabular ordinal classification. Current methods for tabular ordinal classification rely primarily on retrieving similar features and augmenting sample feature representations by fusing features similar to the ordinal distance between classes. However, the existing methods neglect the full utilization of label ordinal knowledge. To address this, a method based on ordinal label entropy optimization is proposed, which effectively guides the model in learning ordinal information by mining the ordinal entropy embedded in the label order knowledge. First, an ordinal entropy calculation module is established that quantifies ordinal entropy based on the rank differences between the predicted and true labels. Through step-by-step analysis and derivation, the ordinal label entropy is designed as a novel rank loss function, which is introduced as a regularization term in the model. This encourages the model to learn the ordinal relationship between labels and reduces information loss caused by unordered predictions. The ordinal entropy optimized ranking loss function is combined with the original loss function of the model to improve its predictive ability. Finally, experiments on multiple ordinal tabular datasets reveal that this method outperforms various baseline models, demonstrating the effectiveness and advantages of the ordinal entropy optimization model in tabular ordinal classification tasks.

title: Quality Estimation for Machine Translation in Low-Resource Settings
abstract: Evaluating the quality of Machine Translation (MT) for low-resource languages is a challenging cross-lingual problem in Natural Language Processing. Quality Estimation (QE) aims to predict MT quality in the absence of reference translations. This thesis investigates QE through multilingual modelling, architectural adaptations, novel data curation and efficient learning strategies across nine low-resource language pairs. First, this thesis analyses how multilingual training influences QE performance, showing that combining linguistically related languages yields consistent improvements over training on a single language pair. The research then examines the suitability of large language models (LLMs) for QE in zero-shot, in-context learning, and fine-tuned settings. While LLMs show broad generalisation ability, empirical analysis reveals limitations in low-resource languages, including inconsistencies in tokenisation and weaker cross-lingual alignment. Results indicate that prompt-based adaptation alone is insufficient for reliable QE for low-resource languages and motivate architectural refinement. Building on this finding, the thesis proposes ALOPE, a regression-aligned framework for adapting decoder-based LLMs by leveraging informative intermediate Transformer layers for QE. Combined with lightweight regression heads and parameter-efficient techniques, ALOPE enables smaller open-weight LLMs to achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple language pairs while operating within memory and compute constraints. Further, this research extends QE beyond scalar prediction by introducing a dataset enriched with human-annotated error descriptions that provide contextual supervision. Building on this, we propose ALOPE-RL, a policy-based reinforcement learning framework that optimises quantised LLMs using multi-component rewards, achieving state-of-the-art performance and remaining effective under extreme data constraints. This thesis shows that QE for low-resource languages can be performed through linguistically grounded multilingual transfer, regression-aligned adaptation, and error-aware reinforcement learning, for practical translation evaluation. All datasets, models, and code are publicly released.

title: Comparative Study of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms for Vision-Based Autonomous Drone Landing Using ArUco Marker
abstract: Autonomous drone landing on visual markers is required for applications like delivery, inspection, and surveillance. In this research, vision-based landing using fiducial ArUco markers is explored in the Microsoft AirSim simulator and the comparison of three deep reinforcement learning algorithms: Deep Q Network (DQN), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and Soft Actor Critic (SAC). All the agents are run under a consistent reward structure that rewards accurate touchdowns and discourages marker loss with only the use of a downwards facing camera. Experiments indicate that PPO has the most stable overall performance, SAC for the best landing accuracy when the marker is always visible, and DQN is more sensitive to variance in the reward. These results provide practical insight into selecting reinforcement learning strategies for real-world UAV landing applications.

title: Utilizing BERTopic modeling for concept discovery in the domain of gerotranscendence and solitude
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ontology development is a complex, iterative process that traditionally requires extensive collaboration between ontology developers and subject matter experts. While effective, this manual approach is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and prone to cognitive bias. To streamline early-stage ontology development and uncover concepts that might be overlooked through manual review alone, we applied automated topic modeling with BERTopic to extract topics, keywords, topic labels, and summaries from The Handbook of Solitude: Psychological Perspectives on Social Isolation, Social Withdrawal, and Being Alone and Gerotranscendence: A Developmental Theory of Positive Aging. The extracted topic labels after review were used as candidate concepts for the Promoting Healthy Aging through Semantic Enrichment of Solitude Research (PHASES) Ontology. METHODS: We implemented and compared two BERTopic pipelines: (1) the default pipeline and (2) a custom preprocessing pipeline incorporating part-of-speech filtering and n-gram tuning. The pipeline is customized to flexibly extract any specified number of topics and keywords based on user-defined parameters. To compare and merge topic modeling outputs across solitude and gerotranscendence, we used semantic embeddings of topic labels, keywords, and summaries from the custom pipeline. Cosine similarity identified semantically matched topic pairs above a set threshold, enabling categorization and integration into a merged conceptual framework that bridges both domains. RESULTS: From the solitude corpus, BERTopic generated 244 initial topics, which, after SMEs review, were refined to 32 high-quality topics with the custom pipeline and 46 with the default pipeline. For the gerotranscendence corpus, the pipeline produced 172 initial topics, refined to 33 with the custom pipeline and 32 with the default pipeline. Across both corpora, BERTopic contributed 90 ontology terms, 52 from the solitude corpus and 38 from the gerotranscendence corpus. Visual evaluations, including keyword score bar charts, hierarchical clustering dendrograms, and BART-generated summaries, revealed that the custom pipeline produced more fine-grained, domain-specific topics, while the default pipeline offered broader thematic coverage and clearer labels. Certain theory-laden concepts, however, required interpretive input from SMEs. CONCLUSIONS: BERTopic provided an efficient, semi-automated approach for identifying candidate ontology terms from domain literature, supporting both breadth and specificity in concept capture. The topics produced by BERTopic modeling uncover underlying latent concepts, serving as a link between raw text data and structured ontology classes. By facilitating the formation of the hierarchical relationships, it exposes a layered semantic structure that is essential for ontology development. Further, integrating semantic similarity analysis across thematic domains revealed conceptual intersections and overlaps, enhancing the semantic foundation of the PHASES Ontology and offering a replicable method for cross-domain ontology development.

title: Cross-layer downgrade-resistant security negotiation for the quantum Internet protocol stack
abstract: The quantum internet is evolving from isolated point-to-point quantum key distribution links toward a globally interconnected, multi-layer protocol stack supporting entanglement distribution, quantum teleportation, and distributed quantum computing. As this architecture matures, each protocol layer-physical, link, network, transport, and application exposes negotiable security parameters: QKD protocol type, entanglement fidelity thresholds, purification rounds, error-correction schemes, and authentication methods. Yet no standardized mechanism exists to negotiate these parameters securely across layers or to prevent adversarial downgrade. The classical internet spent two decades rediscovering this lesson through attacks such as POODLE, FREAK, Logjam, KNOB, and Dragonblood; the quantum internet is now repeating the same architectural oversight. This study introduces QShield , a cross-layer security negotiation framework that binds every layer’s capability commitment into a unified transcript hash, ensuring that any single-layer downgrade invalidates the session-wide security context. We formalize a quantum security downgrade hierarchy spanning six levels from device-independent QKD to classical cryptography and identify twelve concrete downgrade attack vectors mapped from classical analogs. Evaluation across all twelve attack types shows that QShield with cross-layer transcript binding achieves 100% deterministic detection across the twelve modeled downgrade vectors evaluated under emulation, whereas independent per-layer checks detect only 40–60% of coordinated multi-layer attacks. Hybrid mode preserves near-classical session bootstrap latency (48-55 ms versus 25-30 ms baseline), while the signaling overhead remains within practical bounds (3.5-5 KB versus 0.8-1.2 KB for classical).

title: Class visualizations and activation atlases for computational pathology
abstract: The clinical promise of computational pathology increasingly depends on foundation model-based pipelines, yet the morphological concepts encoded by these systems remain poorly understood. We address this gap with a concept-level visualization framework using class visualizations (CVs) and activation atlases (AAs) in a pathology foundation-model setting across colorectal tissue and multi-organ cancer tasks. Four pathologists annotate hematoxylin and eosin-stained image patches as well as generated visualizations, complemented by attribution- and similarity-based metrics. CVs retain class-associated morphology for distinct tissue classes, with reduced separability and higher annotator variability in morphologically overlapping cancer classes. AAs expose layer-dependent organization of encoded concepts, with coherent regions for coarse tissue and cancer groupings and increasing dispersion and overlap at finer label granularities. Together, these findings show that concept-level visualization makes representations learned by pathology foundation models inspectable across diagnostic difficulty levels, with feature separation decreasing and ambiguity increasing as morphological complexity and expert disagreement rise.

title: An improved adaptive optimization approach for mobile agent-based multimodal path planning
abstract: Path planning is a core technology in robotics, autonomous driving systems, and unmanned aerial vehicle navigation. However, in complex environments with multiple constraints, existing intelligent optimization methods are still susceptible to factors such as uneven initial distribution, insufficient environmental feedback, and premature convergence, making it difficult to stably obtain high-quality feasible paths. To address the above problems, this paper proposes an Enhanced Competition of Tribes and Cooperation of Members Method (ECTCM) based on the competition-cooperation search framework of the Competition of Tribes and Cooperation of Members Method (CTCM), aiming to improve the global exploration capability, environmental adaptability, and local exploitation capability in complex path planning tasks. Specifically, this paper designs a double-trigonometric coupled chaotic map and combines it with opposition-based learning to construct a chaotic opposition-based initialization strategy, aiming to improve the distribution uniformity of the initial population and the coverage of the search space. An environmental quality assessment mechanism is proposed to dynamically adjust the intensity of inter-tribal competition and migration according to the environmental quality of different search regions, thereby enhancing the adaptiveness of the search direction. An improved adaptive mutation strategy is introduced to adjust the perturbation intensity based on historical memory and individual ranking information, so as to alleviate population stagnation and premature convergence. Meanwhile, an elite-guided learning evolution strategy is designed to guide inferior individuals using a weighted elite center, thereby strengthening late-stage local exploitation capability. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, this paper compares ECTCM with 11 mainstream optimization algorithms on the CEC2020 (D = 50, 100) and CEC2022 (D = 10, 20) benchmark test functions, and further applies it to two-dimensional (2D) grid and three-dimensional (3D) UAV path planning tasks. The experimental results show that ECTCM achieves the lowest Friedman average rank in all benchmark test scenarios, and its average win rates based on the Wilcoxon rank-sum test reach 89.1%, 92.7%, 79.5%, and 83.3%, respectively. In the path planning experiments, compared with the original CTCM, ECTCM achieves comprehensive improvement rates of 6.84% and 21.36% in the 2D grid map and 3D UAV path planning scenarios, respectively. The above results indicate that, while introducing additional computational overhead, ECTCM can improve path quality, convergence accuracy, and search stability, providing a competitive optimization method for agent path planning in complex simulation environments.

title: AVERT: Audio-Verified Adjudication for Spoken Dialogue State Tracking
abstract: Spoken dialogue state tracking recovers slot-value pairs from speech, where ASR errors concentrate in entity values and persist across turns, making it both a generation and an editing problem. A strong per-turn text editor corrects much of this but, operating on the transcript alone, leaves three recoverable errors: a value predicted inconsistently across turns, an omitted slot, and a value the audio does not support. We present AVERT, which scores each candidate value by combining cross-turn agreement with a trained audio-conditioned verifier and resolves the three error types with three operators, vote, add, and swap, each restricted to the slots where its error is common. On SpokenWOZ, a base speech-LLM reaches 33.04 JGA, a text editor 38.34, and AVERT 40.13, without retraining either. This is in the range of a 1B end-to-end system that consumes the full spoken history (39.32), though AVERT uses two 1B decoders rather than one. The audio verifier contributes a statistically significant gain, and restricting each operator to a selected slot subset matters: removing it lets unrestricted voting overwrite correct categorical values and fall below the editor.

title: Semantic-Guided Multimodal Preprocessing for Vision Transformer-Based Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma Grading
abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (CCRCC) grading is essential for treatment planning, yet existing approaches either analyze patch-level images directly or focus solely on nuclei-level classification, without linking to final tumor grading. We propose a semantic-guided multimodal preprocessing method that integrates nuclei classification maps from existing pre-trained models with RGB histopathology images for Vision Transformer (ViT)-based CCRCC grading. Our approach employs classification map channel concatenation and multiplicative modulation, with optimized overlays to leverage nuclei grading information, while preserving RGB textural features. Evaluation of multiple preprocessing strategies demonstrates that semantic-guided enhancement achieves 0.916 balanced accuracy, outperforming RGB-only baseline (0.707) and max-voting aggregation from prior studies (0.427). Sensitivity analysis reveals that this 21 percentage point improvement over baseline persists even under simulated perturbation at rates matching current state-of-the-art nuclei classification model error thresholds, suggesting both effective semantic utilization and practical robustness. These findings show that preprocessing-based multimodal fusion can leverage the diagnostic potential of existing imperfect nuclei classifiers, effectively bridging previously isolated fine-grained nuclear-level analysis with coarse-grained ViT-based patch classification. Per-class recall was consistent across grades (0.93, 0.91, 0.91), indicating that gains are not concentrated in the majority class. Because the sensitivity analysis perturbs ground-truth maps rather than predictions from an actual nuclei model, this result characterizes robustness under simulated error rather than deployment with a real upstream model, which remains for future work.

title: A Unified Uncertainty-Aware Back-End for Speaker Verification: Scoring, Normalization, and Calibration
abstract: Speaker verification back-ends commonly combine similarity scoring, score normalization, and calibration. However, speaker embeddings extracted from real-world utterances have trial-dependent reliability because of factors such as duration, noise, and channel variation. Existing uncertainty-aware methods primarily improve the speaker encoder or the initial similarity score, while the estimated uncertainty is typically not propagated through subsequent normalization and calibration. We represent each utterance by a speaker embedding, interpreted as a posterior mean, together with its covariance as an uncertainty estimate. We present a unified uncertainty-aware back-end comprising uncertainty-aware cosine scoring, uncertainty-aware AS-Norm (UAS-Norm), and uncertainty-aware Quality Measure Function calibration (UQMF). Covariance information is incorporated throughout this pipeline to adjust score scaling, cohort statistics, normalized-score combination, and calibration features. Experiments with ECAPA-TDNN and ResNet show consistent EER reductions and improved target--non-target separation across both architectures.

title: Audio-Text Cross-Attention with Psycholinguistic Support Features for Ambivalence/Hesitancy Recognition
abstract: We present a frame-independent audio-text system for the 3rd Ambivalence/Hesitancy Video Recognition Challenge at the 11th Affective & Behavior Analysis in-the-Wild (ABAW) Workshop. Videos are divided into overlapping 5-s windows aligned with transcript timestamps. Each window combines prosodic audio descriptors, emotion-oriented RoBERTa embeddings, and 74 psycholinguistic features representing uncertainty, hedging, and attitudinal conflict. Temporal cross-attention fuses audio and text, while the support features condition gated Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) pooling. A five-seed ensemble achieves an average precision of 0.875 and a macro-F1 of 0.722 on the 525-video labeled public-test split. Notably, our submission ranked third overall on the official challenge leaderboard, with a macro-F1 of 0.7455. Source code is available at https://github.com/Liga-de-IA-PUCPR/abaw-11-ah-challenge/.

title: Experimental Investigation of the Effect of Dispersion on Squeezing Generation in a Synchronously Pumped Optical Parametric Oscillator
abstract: ABSTRACT An experimental investigation of intracavity dispersion effects in a synchronously pumped optical parametric oscillator (SPOPO) is presented. A flexible setup combining spectral and phase shaping of both pump and local oscillator fields with frequency‐resolved balanced homodyne detection is employed to examine how intracavity dispersion influences squeezing. Different cavity configurations with varying finesse and dispersion conditions are studied, and the squeezing is measured as a function of pump power and local oscillator bandwidth. Contrary to expectations based on existing theoretical models, the measured squeezing levels remain essentially unchanged as dispersion varies. To account for these observations, a modeling approach is introduced in which intracavity dispersion is described as an effective spectral filtering occurring at the stage of SPOPO supermode generation. Within this framework, the filtering is incorporated directly into the interaction Hamiltonian of the nonlinear process. This perspective establishes a consistent experimental benchmark for the study of dispersion in SPOPOs and underscores the importance of spectral filtering in the interpretation of multimode squeezing experiments.

title: DIPS II: A Theory of Compact System Information
abstract: From Source Resolved Systems to Certified Computation This article introduces DIPS-information: a compact, source-resolved and task-sufficient form of system information designed to serve simultaneously as a formal description, a computational representation and an interpretable basis for inference. A DIPS representation is compact not because it merely stores fewer symbols, but because it retains exactly the distinctions required by a declared task while keeping their source meaning and computational role explicit. We define a finite DIPS realization as an admissible source-resolved link list with channel laws and memories, a composition grammar, an uncertainty specification and a requested output. On that common object we develop exact sufficiency certificates, conflict witnesses for missing distinctions, composition and distribution laws, and a source-preserving condition for certified computation. The result is a theory of the passage from interacting reality to compact system information and then to a licensed calculation; it does not claim universal data compression, quantum advantage or a completed device experiment. This is the second article in the DIPS (Dynamic Identifiable Spatial Links) programme, following "DIPS: The Channel Configuration Is the Quantum Assignment", https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22107929 . The verification supplement is the companion repository https://github.com/AlexMiroff/dips2-verification-code , snapshot release v1.0.0: https://github.com/AlexMiroff/dips2-verification-code/releases/tag/v1.0.0 , which holds the theory factories for Sections 6.1, 6.2, 6.4, 6, 7.7, 8.5, 9.5, 10.5, 11.5, 12.6 and 13.6, the Appendix A sign-law check, the consolidated closure report, and the Section 6.1 CSV, report and Figures 2 and 3. Each factory writes a machine-readable JSON report. The QUBO check in Section 10.5 verifies a classical encoding condition only, and the repository reports no quantum-device result.

title: Code and data for: Test population or validation design? Decomposing the group-holdout penalty in deferred-label quality prediction
abstract: Reproducibility package for the article "Test population or validation design? Decomposing the group-holdout penalty in deferred-label quality prediction". The package regenerates every number, table and figure in the article from the public source data. It carries no data of its own. The acquisition script downloads the published cell arrays at run time, so the archive stays small and the provenance of the data stays with its original publisher. Five steps run from a single entry point: data acquisition, feature building, the main analysis, a group-boundary diagnostic, and figure generation. A pinned environment specification and SHA-256 checksums for the three generated result files are included, so a reader can verify a quoted number without running anything, or re-run and confirm the output matches. The benchmark uses 124 public lithium iron phosphate cells cycled in three batches. It compares validation designs for grouped manufacturing data while holding the scored population, the training budget and the fitting procedure fixed, which separates a change of test population from a change in the units a model saw during training. Changes in version 1.2.0 Added src/group_shift.py, a descriptive diagnostic reporting where the 40 group B cells sit relative to the 84 group A cells in the nine-feature space. It reports Mahalanobis distances against the group A reference, cross-validated separability with a label-permutation null, and a group A principal component basis with group B projected onto it. It fits no model of lifetime, and nothing else in the pipeline reads its output. Added results/group_shift.json, the frozen output of that step, with its checksum. The diagnostic answers a reviewer question about the main null result: group B is distinguishable from group A, so the comparison is not degenerate, but 39 of its 40 cells lie inside the range group A spans, so the null is not a failure to extrapolate. Renamed throughout from "Online Resource 1" to "Additional file 1", and the target journal updated to Journal of Big Data. The archive root folder is now AdditionalFile1/. No change to the feature definitions, the models, the estimands, the tests or any number published in version 1.1.0. title: Native unknown Outputs as a Scheduling Signal for Model Arrays: Small-Model Gatekeeping, Queryable Knowledge Maps, and the Failure Boundary of Same-Family Weighted Voting (English v1.1)
abstract: Companion short paper to "A 774M-Parameter Model Trained from Scratch Says 'I Don't Know'" (10.5281/zenodo.22191510). Moving the uncertainty signal from post-hoc estimation to generation time: unknown as a first-class output category becomes a metadata bit that a model array amplifies into three system capabilities — gatekeeping (37× leakage suppression; out-of-domain perception holds on all 55 concepts of a three-gradient probe set, with root shortcuts inert outside the boundary band), a queryable knowledge map (cross-seed consistency 0.946, disagreement self-localizing to the known/unknown critical band), and union-intersection two-expert routing (3,000-step unit expansion, zero forgetting). A clean negative result bounds the signal's value: within a same-family array, equal/quality/oracle weighting and two further fusion operations all degenerate to identical decisions (0.976) — while a single rule unit carrying out-of-array information lifts the same probe set to 41/41: overriding power requires out-of-array information sources (measured, M4v3). A six-route industry survey finds no counterpart for the native-metadata-bit + small-model-gatekeeper + state-judgment-array combination. v1.1 (2026-09-01): back-fills M4v3 heterogeneous overriding (41/41) and M2c sharp-boundary probes (11/12; first lexical-classification failure instance). Preregistered; negative details reported as-is. This record is the v1.1 of 10.5281/zenodo.22220040, published as a new deposition due to a Zenodo new-version pipeline fault.

title: Quantum Topological Optimization for Hidden Computation
abstract: Quantum Topological Optimization (QTO) offers a novel approach to enhancing the security of quantum computation by leveraging the principles of topological geometry. This paper investigates the potential of QTO to improve key generation and security within quantum-encrypted systems. We present a comprehensive theoretical framework and initial explorations of algorithm implementation, demonstrating a significant improvement in key generation security compared to traditional methods. The core mechanism centers around the application of a customized topological optimization algorithm to key generation, resulting in enhanced resilience against various attacks. The study highlights the advantages of this approach in safeguarding quantum information, particularly in the context of dynamic and complex cryptographic protocols.

title: Messages Passed Along the Edges: A Contemporary Synthesis Review of Graph Neural Networks for Relational Data
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Graph Neural Networks for Relational Data in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of GNN and graph learning as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Cape Grysbok: A Novel Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm Inspired by the Agile Movement of Cape Grysboks
abstract: This paper introduces Cape Grysbok, a new metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the observed movement patterns of Cape Grysboks ( *Cynarctus villosus* ), a nimble and agile antelope species endemic to the Western Cape region of South Africa. The algorithm leverages the grybok's ability to rapidly change direction, adapt to varying terrain, and efficiently search for food sources as its core principles. Cape Grysbok combines elements of Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Adaptive Memory Search (AMS) with a novel dynamic inertia weight adjustment mechanism. Specifically, the inertia weight is adjusted based on the grybok's observed acceleration and deceleration patterns – mimicking its ability to quickly shift momentum. Furthermore, a memory component is implemented to retain promising solutions, guided by the grybok's tendency to revisit areas with potential rewards. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through a series of benchmark test functions, demonstrating its effectiveness in solving complex optimization problems. The experimental results indicate that Cape Grysbok exhibits competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic algorithms like PSO and AMS, showcasing its potential as a viable optimization tool.

title: Contextualized Kernel Learning for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to unsupervised domain adaptation leveraging kernel learning, termed Contextualized Kernel Learning (CKL). The core idea is to address the limitations of traditional static kernel methods by dynamically adapting the kernel function based on the contextual information present in each data instance. We propose a mechanism utilizing a recurrent neural network (RNN) to generate a "context vector" representing the current data. This context vector is then employed to adjust the parameters of a pre-defined kernel function, effectively tailoring the kernel to the specific characteristics of the data. We demonstrate that this dynamic adaptation significantly improves the performance of kernel methods in unsupervised domain adaptation scenarios. The key innovation lies in the iterative, context-aware adjustment of the kernel, offering a more robust and effective solution compared to static kernel approaches. Our experiments highlight the advantages of CKL across various benchmark datasets.

title: Cao-vit: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Crested Gibbon Social Dynamics
abstract: This paper introduces Cao-vit, a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the complex social dynamics observed in Crested Gibbons ( *Nomascus crasus*). Crested Gibbons exhibit remarkable coordinated movement and decision-making within their troops, demonstrating a sophisticated form of collective intelligence. Cao-vit leverages these observed behaviors – particularly the "cresting" movement pattern and the hierarchical structure within the troop – to design a new metaheuristic approach for solving optimization problems. The algorithm incorporates three key components: a dynamic population of solutions, a 'cresting' movement strategy for exploring the search space, and a hierarchical ranking system to guide convergence. Mathematical formulations are presented to detail these components, including the population update equation (1), the movement probability calculation (2), and the ranking mechanism (3). The algorithm's performance is evaluated across a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential for applications in diverse fields. The core innovation lies in translating the observed social structure of the Crested Gibbon into a robust and adaptable optimization strategy.

title: California Leaf-nosed Bat Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the "California Leaf-nosed Bat Algorithm" (CLBA), inspired by the foraging behavior of *Corynorhinus townsendii* (California leaf-nosed bat). These bats exhibit remarkable efficiency in locating food sources in complex and dynamic environments. The CLBA algorithm leverages this foraging strategy, incorporating elements of exploration and exploitation, to effectively solve complex optimization problems. The core of the algorithm revolves around a bat population, each representing a potential solution. Bat movement is governed by a combination of random exploration and gradient-based exploitation, mimicking the bats' flight patterns and echolocation. The algorithm employs a fitness evaluation function to assess the quality of each solution, and a convergence criterion based on population diversity and solution improvement. The performance of the CLBA algorithm is evaluated on a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness and competitive nature compared to established metaheuristic algorithms. The algorithm's parameters are carefully tuned to achieve optimal performance. The results show that CLBA is a promising approach for a variety of complex optimization challenges.

title: ## Brown Dog-faced Bat: A Novel Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic optimization algorithm, termed "Brown Dog-faced Bat" (BDB), inspired by the foraging behavior of brown dog-faced bats ( *Craseonycteris thonglongyai*). These bats utilize a unique echolocation strategy, navigating complex environments by emitting ultrasonic calls and interpreting the returning echoes. BDB mimics this process through a multi-dimensional search space, employing a combination of position updates, frequency modulation, and a dynamic exploration-exploitation balance. The algorithm's core mechanism revolves around a 'dog-faced' representation of the bat's search, where each bat's position and frequency are dynamically adjusted based on the received echo strength. This paper details the algorithm's design, its mathematical formulation, and demonstrates its effectiveness through simulations on benchmark optimization problems. The results indicate that BDB exhibits competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic algorithms, particularly in problems requiring complex exploration and fine-tuning. The algorithm's adaptability and ability to escape local optima are key strengths. Further research will focus on refining the algorithm's parameters and exploring its applicability to diverse real-world optimization challenges.

title: Quantum Chaotic Generator and Approximation of Multivariate Functions
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum chaotic generators (QCGs) for efficient approximation of multivariate functions and their application in quantum numerical simulations. The core claim is that the inherent randomness of a QCG can be leveraged to generate high-dimensional chaotic sequences, which can then be utilized as approximate samples for multivariate functions. The proposed mechanism relies on quantum measurements and entanglement to construct the QCG, and subsequently, the generated chaotic sequences are used as proxies for evaluating complex multivariate functions. This approach offers a novel method for numerical computation, particularly relevant within the context of quantum computing. The theoretical framework presented here outlines the design principles and potential benefits of this strategy, emphasizing its role in accelerating and potentially enhancing numerical simulations of various problems. We demonstrate the feasibility of this method through a theoretical analysis, focusing on the key aspects of sequence generation and function approximation. The ultimate goal is to provide a foundational understanding for future research in this emerging field.

title: Quantum State Adaptive Topology Transformation
abstract: Quantum state adaptive topology transformation is a novel approach to quantum computing that utilizes the inherent adaptability of quantum states to manipulate the topology of quantum systems. This paper explores the development of a method that leverages this adaptability to enable complex quantum computations and algorithms, offering potential advantages over existing techniques. We detail the core mechanism, outlining how quantum state transformations are employed to reshape the underlying topology, ultimately facilitating enhanced computational capabilities. The research highlights the benefits of this approach, focusing on its ability to address challenges associated with numerical issues and provide more complex topological operations.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Self-Adaptation Algorithm (DASA)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Adaptive Self-Adaptation Algorithm (DASA), a novel computational framework designed to automatically optimize algorithm parameters for enhanced performance. The core of DASA lies in its dynamic parameter adjustment strategy, driven by a learning-based approach that adapts to runtime performance metrics. Unlike traditional optimization methods that rely on predefined parameter sets, DASA learns and adjusts algorithm parameters in real-time, enabling a more flexible and efficient optimization process. The paper details the algorithm's implementation, explores its impact on performance, and provides a comprehensive analysis of its capabilities. The research highlights the advantages of DASA in scenarios requiring rapid adaptation and continuous improvement of algorithm performance.

title: Bonobo: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Bonobo Social Dynamics
abstract: This paper presents Bonobo, a novel metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the social dynamics observed in bonobo communities. Bonobo leverages the concept of dominance hierarchies and coalition formation, common in bonobo societies, to guide the search process. The algorithm incorporates a 'dominance' mechanism to prioritize promising solutions, a 'coalition' component to foster collaborative exploration, and a 'stability' factor to prevent premature convergence. Bonobo's design aims to improve the robustness and efficiency of traditional metaheuristic methods, particularly in complex, multi-modal optimization landscapes. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on a range of benchmark functions, demonstrating competitive results against established metaheuristics like Simulated Annealing and Genetic Algorithms. The core of Bonobo lies in its adaptive population management strategy, which dynamically adjusts the population size and diversity based on the current search state. Finally, we provide a detailed explanation of the algorithm's parameters, their influence on performance, and future research directions.

title: Adaptive Bayesian Networks for Risk Assessment and Prediction
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to risk assessment and prediction utilizing Adaptive Bayesian Networks (ABNs). Traditional Bayesian networks often rely on manually tuned parameters, limiting their adaptability and potentially hindering accurate risk evaluation and prediction. Our proposed model dynamically adjusts its parameters based on historical data and environmental changes, resulting in enhanced predictive capabilities, particularly within the domains of financial risk assessment and fraud detection. The core mechanism centers around a "self-adaptive parameter adjustment" process, ensuring the network's performance remains optimized for the specific context. This paper details the design of the ABN, the implementation of the adjustment mechanism, and the results demonstrating its improved performance compared to existing methods. The focus is on providing a robust and adaptable framework for risk management across diverse applications.

title: # Blazed Luzon Chrotomys: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Foraging Behavior of *Chrotomys gonzalez-pacheti*
abstract: This paper presents Blazed Luzon Chrotomys (BLC), a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of the Luzon Blazed Rat (*Chrotomys gonzalez-pacheti*). The algorithm leverages the observed adaptive strategies of this rodent – specifically, its tendency to blaze a trail through the environment, prioritizing areas with higher resource density – to efficiently navigate complex optimization landscapes. BLC incorporates a dynamic trail-blazing mechanism, a probabilistic exploration phase, and a local search strategy that mimics the rat's selective foraging. The algorithm's performance is evaluated across a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions with promising convergence rates. We detail the algorithm's design, provide mathematical formulations, and showcase its capabilities through simulations, establishing BLC as a viable alternative within the metaheuristic optimization toolbox.

title: gistUFO: An Alignment of gist and gUFO
abstract: gist is Semantic Arts’ upper-level business-oriented ontology. Used as a starting point for domain ontologies across a wide variety of fields, gist is designed to be lightweight and easily adaptable. gUFO is an OWL-DL compliant implementation of the Unified Foundational Ontology (UFO), an upper ontology developed by the Ontology & Conceptual Modeling Research Group (NEMO). UFO, like gist, has been adapted for several uses, with its strong theoretical foundations making it an ideal resource for developing and evaluating more specialized models. gist, with many past implementations across enterprise use cases, is well suited to business applications, but does not have the same theoretical foundations as UFO (and therefore gUFO). gUFO’s implementation of UFO in OWL provides a simple way to analyze ontologies for alignment with UFO. We demonstrate this capacity by mapping gist classes to both the gUFO Individuals and Types hierarchies, by subclass and instantiation relationships respectively. Aligning the two ontologies has several benefits: it enables interoperability between gist and gUFO-based ontologies, verifies the ontological foundations of gist, enables the use of several UFO-based validation queries, and provides a UFO- and gist-compliant starting point for those wishing to develop ontologies that align with both. This paper contains our mappings, an explanation of our processes, the rationale behind certain mapping decisions, and our suggestions for future work.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Strategies for LLM-Based Text-to-SQL Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: This OSF project documents the protocol, methodological audit trail, and reproducibility materials for the systematic literature review “Retrieval-Augmented Strategies for LLM-Based Text-to-SQL Systems: A Systematic Literature Review.” The review characterizes how retrieval-augmented strategies are designed and empirically evaluated in large language model (LLM)-based Text-to-SQL systems. It focuses on approaches that dynamically retrieve contextual information—such as database schemas, values, natural language–SQL examples, documentation, domain knowledge, or other structured knowledge—and use the retrieved information to support SQL generation, reasoning, decomposition, refinement, validation, or correction. The review covers peer-reviewed journal articles published in English within a search window from January 2022 to August 19, 2026. Systematic searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore. Eligible studies were required to investigate natural-language-to-SQL generation, directly involve an LLM in the Text-to-SQL pipeline, incorporate a retrieval-augmented mechanism according to the predefined operational definition, and report an empirical evaluation. The review addresses four research dimensions: (1) the retrieval strategies and types of contextual information used; (2) the LLMs, datasets, database domains, and experimental configurations employed; (3) the evaluation metrics, baselines, and reported effects of retrieval on effectiveness and efficiency; and (4) recurrent limitations, implementation challenges, and open research gaps. The definitive searches identified 110 database records. After cross-source deduplication, 61 unique records entered title-and-abstract screening. Thirty records were retained for full-text assessment, all of which were successfully retrieved. Full-text eligibility assessment resulted in 24 included studies and 6 exclusions. Study selection was conducted using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, with independent reviewer assessment and reconciliation procedures documented in the project audit materials. Pilot searches and calibration activities were conducted before the definitive review stages to refine the search strategy and eligibility framework. These pilot activities are maintained separately from the formal study-selection dataset and are not included in the reported review counts. The resulting evidence synthesis characterizes retrieval according to four complementary analytical dimensions—WHAT is retrieved, HOW retrieval is performed, WHERE retrieval intervenes in the Text-to-SQL pipeline, and WHY retrieval is introduced. The project also documents the review’s data-extraction framework, quality assessment, retrieval-specific evidence synthesis, limitations, and reproducibility materials. Because the definitive database searches had already been executed when the OSF project was made public, this project should not be interpreted as a fully prospective preregistration of all review stages. It serves as a public protocol, methodological audit trail, and repository for the review’s reproducibility materials.

title: Energy analysis of bifacial photovoltaic systems on different soils and orientations in a coastal low-latitude area
abstract: Coastal low-latitude regions exhibit consistent annual solar irradiance, offering stable solar resource availability that enhances their suitability for year-round photovoltaic energy generation. This study analyzes the annual energy production of bifacial photovoltaic (PV) systems under varying ground albedo conditions and installation orientations, accounting for the effects of tilt angle, ground clearance height, ground coverage ratio (GCR), and row spacing. Meteorological parameters were derived from Japan's Himawari-8/9 satellite data, which were integrated into the System Advisor Model and the National Renewable Energy Laboratory database to compute front‑ and rear‑side solar irradiance. Electrical measurements from bifacial PV systems were used to evaluate annual energy output and bifacial gain. Results demonstrate that landscape-oriented bifacial PV systems consistently outperformed portrait-oriented configurations in both energy production and bifacial gain. For systems with optimized parameters, landscape orientations achieved annual energy outputs 0.70%, 0.51%, and 0.42% higher than portrait orientations for white dry sands, white sands with granite rocks, and white wet sand substrates, respectively. Similarly, bifacial gain values for landscape-oriented systems reached 18.64%, 15.47%, and 12.43% across these substrates, surpassing portrait-oriented systems. The findings highlight the crucial influence of ground albedo and panel orientation on optimizing the performance of bifacial photovoltaic systems in coastal low‑latitude regions.

title: Transformer encoder and ensemble learning-based deepfake audio detector using mel-frequency cepstral coefficients
abstract: : While speech spoofing detection techniques based on deep learning have performed well in the recent years, many deep learning-based speech spoofing detection methods based on convolutional neural networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), and Transformer based architectures have difficulty in effectively representing discriminative local acoustic features and long-range dependencies, which reduces their resistance to the sophisticated attacks of synthesized and voice converted speech. To overcome these disadvantages, we introduce a new detector for automatic speech spoofing detection, which is called Transformer Encoder and Ensemble Learning-based Detector (TEEL-Det). The proposed framework combines the ensemble learning, Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), and Transformer Encoder to improve the representation of features and contextual modeling. The ensemble learning module extracts the complementary discriminative features and the MFCCs give compact and informative acoustic speech representations from raw speech. The Transformer Encoder uses a self-attention mechanism to learn the characteristics of the speech that are of interest for accurate classification of bonafide and spoofed speech while maintaining long range dependencies. The proposed model was tested on a subset of the Logical Access (LA) category of the ASVspoof 2019 challenge, which includes synthesized speech and voice converted speech. Through experimental results, the effectiveness and robustness of TEEL-Det are clearly shown in speech spoofing detection, and its performance is better than that of other methods, with an Equal Error Rate (EER) of 0.003% for the LA evaluation set.

title: A Three‐Qubit Ising Hamiltonian For High‐Efficiency Quantum Energy Teleportation on Superconducting Hardware
abstract: ABSTRACT Quantum Energy Teleportation (QET) leverages quantum entanglement to transfer energy between two distant locations without physically moving it. The first realization of QET on superconducting hardware, a 2‐qubit system, demonstrated about work efficiency (work relative to the deposited energy). Here we introduce a 3‐qubit approach that enhances QET's energy efficiency through a novel 3‐qubit ground state Ising Model Hamiltonian satisfying zero mean energy and anti‐commutation constraints on the sender and receiver observables. We study two protocols. In the Single‐Input Multiple‐Output (SIMO) model, a single sender (Alice) deposits energy and two receivers (Bob and Charlie) jointly extract negative energy; with every interaction term retained, including the inter‐receiver bond, the honest efficiency is to , comparable to the of the minimal 2‐qubit model but now shared by two outputs. In the Multiple‐Input Single‐Output (MISO) model, two senders (Alice and Charlie) deposit a combined energy through a single entangle‐then‐measure measurement and a single receiver (Bob) extracts it, giving a net teleportation efficiency of to , well above the 2‐qubit value, with energy conservation respected. The negative energy density at the receiver is the protocol's signature.

title: MERGED: Multimodal Entity Resolution via Generated Expert Reasoning Distillation
abstract: In product entity resolution, relationship definitions constantly evolve with business needs, yet adapting to each change traditionally requires slow, costly human annotation that is often noisy and carries no reasoning. Large vision-language models (VLMs) prompted zero-shot can adapt to a new definition immediately and supply the reasoning that human labels lack, but their cost and latency are prohibitive at production scale. We present MERGED, a distillation framework that transfers not just labels but structured reasoning from large teacher VLMs into a compact 7B-parameter student, requiring no human annotation. Multiple teachers label each product pair and articulate the reasoning behind their decision: agreement pairs supply supervised fine-tuning, while disagreements are resolved by a meta-judge into preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization. Evaluated against human-labeled ground truth on a multilingual e-commerce dataset, the resulting student improves PR-AUC by 13.79% over the same backbone trained on human labels and surpasses the larger Qwen2.5-32B-VL baseline by 6.32% at 6x lower cost, while also yielding tighter label-reasoning alignment (over 10% above Qwen2.5-32B-VL). Moreover, re-applying MERGED from an existing checkpoint adapts to a new relationship definition with only 10K samples, improving PR-AUC by 6.97% over zero-shot and outperforming from-scratch training. MERGED enables rapid adaptation to evolving relationship definitions, supporting a new one in days rather than months, at a cost and latency suitable for large-scale industrial deployment.

title: Rethinking Learnability in Offline Data-driven Optimization
abstract: Black-Box Optimization (BBO) has broad applications, while traditional algorithms such as evolutionary algorithms and Bayesian optimization face efficiency challenges as real-world BBO problems grow increasingly complex. Data-driven optimization has been the most popular paradigm to improve the efficiency of BBO, by learning from data. Offline data-driven optimization seeks high-quality solutions using only a fixed set of previous evaluations, attracting substantial attention because it requires no additional online evaluations. Many offline optimization methods have been proposed, but a fundamental question remains unanswered: what learnability is sufficient for offline optimization? Prior theoretical studies show that Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learnability is insufficient, as the optimal region may remain poorly learned even when most regions are well learned. In this paper, we propose algorithm-dependent learnability, which requires accuracy only on the optimizer's trajectory. We prove that its value-query form is sufficient for representative discrete settings, including greedy and local search for submodular maximization, while its first-order analogue is sufficient for projected gradient descent on convex minimization. Motivated by this notion, we formalize a trajectory-learning framework comprising trajectory construction, trajectory modeling, and candidate generation, and analyze existing trajectory-based methods under it. We further propose Uncertainty-aware Gradient-guided Trajectory Learning (UGTL), which constructs locally coherent improvement trajectories reflecting plausible search paths, models them with conditional diffusion, and selects a diverse candidate set. Our experiments show that UGTL achieves the best average rank, 3.1/25, among 25 methods on Design-Bench tasks, and confirm that our trajectory construction plays a significant role in the improvement.

evidence.title: Rethinking Learnability in Offline Data-driven Optimization
evidence.abstract: Black-Box Optimization (BBO) has broad applications, while traditional algorithms such as evolutionary algorithms and Bayesian optimization face efficiency challenges as real-world BBO problems grow increasingly complex. Data-driven optimization has been the most popular paradigm to improve the efficiency of BBO, by learning from data. Offline data-driven optimization seeks high-quality solutions using only a fixed set of previous evaluations, attracting substantial attention because it requires no additional online evaluations. Many offline optimization methods have been proposed, but a fundamental question remains unanswered: what learnability is sufficient for offline optimization? Prior theoretical studies show that Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learnability is insufficient, as the optimal region may remain poorly learned even when most regions are well learned. In this paper, we propose algorithm-dependent learnability, which requires accuracy only on the optimizer's trajectory. We prove that its value-query form is sufficient for representative discrete settings, including greedy and local search for submodular maximization, while its first-order analogue is sufficient for projected gradient descent on convex minimization. Motivated by this notion, we formalize a trajectory-learning framework comprising trajectory construction, trajectory modeling, and candidate generation, and analyze existing trajectory-based methods under it. We further propose Uncertainty-aware Gradient-guided Trajectory Learning (UGTL), which constructs locally coherent improvement trajectories reflecting plausible search paths, models them with conditional diffusion, and selects a diverse candidate set. Our experiments show that UGTL achieves the best average rank, 3.1/25, among 25 methods on Design-Bench tasks, and confirm that our trajectory construction plays a significant role in the improvement.

title: Coding for Multiple Reverse-Complement and Palindromic Duplications
abstract: Reverse-complement (RC) and palindromic (PAL) duplications copy a length-$k$ block, reverse the copy, and insert it immediately after the original block; an RC duplication also complements the copied symbols. We study $q$-ary codes correcting $t$ such operations performed sequentially, so a later operation may copy symbols created by an earlier one. For fixed $q\geq2$ and $k,t\geq1$, every length-$n$ code $C$ for either channel satisfies $n-\log_q|C|\geq t\log_q n-O_{q,k,t}(1)$; for fixed $q,k$ and $1\leq t=t(n)=o(n)$ the lower bound is $t\log_q(n/t)-O_{q,k}(t)$. For a single RC error over an even alphabet with a fixed-point-free complement, the previously known RC-specific construction applies at odd $k$ and does not cover even $k$. For every even $k$ and any involutive complement, we give a coordinate-wise bijection that turns each RC duplication into a PAL duplication. Applying this bijection to every codeword therefore converts any $t$-error-correcting RC code into a PAL code of the same size, and conversely; encoders and decoders transfer by adding linear-time coordinate passes. For every even $k$, we also determine the maximum number of distinct descendants produced by exactly two errors from one source word. Words alternating between any two distinct alphabet symbols attain this maximum for PAL, and the bijection gives the RC maximizers. For both PAL and RC at fixed even $k$, we prove the existence of two-error-correcting codes with redundancy $4\log_q n+O_{q,k}(1)$. In the binary two-error problem, the converse gives $2\log_2 n-O_k(1)$, leaving a factor-two gap in the best existence bounds.

title: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Academic Texts
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems use the question-answering capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to access information outside their parameters. We evaluate if cluster-based semantic chunking improves retrieval and answer quality compared to fixed-size and recursive chunking evaluating on long, structured academic theses using the Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment (RAGAs) framework. RAGAs based faithfulness shows limited reliability in this setup. Performance on fixed versus document specific questions varied substantially, likely related to the formatting of documents and preprocessing. Under the tested configuration, cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler strategies.

title: Can LLMs Imagine Moral Alternatives Beyond Binary Dilemmas?
abstract: As LLMs increasingly serve as moral advisors and agents, they must address conflicts between competing values. Yet prior work on moral dilemmas overlooks a central aspect of human moral cognition: imagining alternatives beyond the given options. We introduce MoralAltDataset, comprising 307 Advisor and AI-facing Agent dilemmas augmented with compromise and reframed alternatives. We compare human and LLM judgments in binary and four-option settings. Across human participants and 15 LLMs, aggregate moral choice distributions differ substantially between the two settings, with compromise often preferred over either original binary option. Results show value shifts and stronger human-LLM agreement on alternatives. Source-stratified results reveal a descriptive gap: human alternative-selection rates are similar across authoring sources, whereas LLMs select GPT-5-authored alternatives substantially more often. We then compare human-authored alternatives with outputs from three representative LLMs through pairwise preference and expert-based evaluations. Alternatives from these LLMs are generally preferred and better satisfy fine-grained structural and ethical criteria, while revealing a trade-off between structural quality and practical feasibility. Our dataset is available here: https://huggingface.co/datasets/jongchanch/MoralAltDataset, and our project page is here: https://jongchanchoi.com/moral-imagination
